name: Uzbekistan
summary: The most populous Central Asian country, heir to the Silk Road cities of Samarkand, Bukhara and Khiva; Soviet until 1991.

location.value: Central Asia; area 448,978 km²; capital and largest city Tashkent.

terrain.value: The Kyzylkum desert and Ustyurt plateau, the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers, irrigated oases, and the Fergana Valley in the east.

climate.value: Continental and dry, with very hot summers, cold winters and little rain.

resources.value: Cotton, gold (including the huge Muruntau mine), natural gas, uranium and copper.

disasters.value: The shrinking of the Aral Sea, caused by Soviet irrigation from the 1960s, left salt and dust storms in Karakalpakstan.

urbanisation.value: About half the population lives in cities; Tashkent is the capital and largest, followed by Samarkand, Namangan and Andijan.

disease.value: Health problems around the Aral Sea, and tuberculosis; hospitals vary widely in quality.

migration.value: Millions of Uzbeks work abroad, mainly in Russia and Kazakhstan, sending money home.

economicBase.value: A major cotton producer and exporter; it mines about 80 tonnes of gold a year (7th in the world); Uzbekneftegaz produces 60–70 billion cubic metres of gas a year; almost 10% of the labour force works abroad.

tradeRoutes.value: Rail and road links across Central Asia, gas pipelines to China, and the old Silk Road cities.

moneyAndTax.value: The Uzbek som, introduced in 1994; currency exchange was freed in 2017.

inequality.value: Large gaps between the capital and rural areas.

governmentType.value: A unitary semi-presidential republic with a two-chamber Oliy Majlis; Islam Karimov was president from 1991 to his death in 2016, then Shavkat Mirziyoyev.

keyRulers.value: Islam Karimov was elected first president on 29 December 1991 and died on 2 September 2016; Shavkat Mirziyoyev became interim president and was elected with 88.6% of the vote.

succession.value: Presidential elections, generally without strong rivals; after Karimov’s death in 2016, power passed peacefully.

institutions.value: A strong presidency, a two-chamber parliament (Oliy Majlis), and neighbourhood councils (mahallas).

stability.value: At Andijan in 2005 troops fired on protesters: 187 killed by official reports, several hundred by unofficial and witness accounts.

eliteConflict.value: Competition between political parties and leaders.

armyAndTech.value: Armed forces built from Soviet units, one of the larger militaries in Central Asia.

majorWars.value: No wars are described. Troops fired into crowds at Andijan in 2005, killing 187 by official count and several hundred by witness accounts. The 1999–2000 incursions are not covered in the part read.

territoryChange.value: Most of Central Asia was gradually absorbed by the Russian Empire during the 19th century (the page does not give 1865 for Tashkent); the Uzbek SSR was created on 27 October 1924.

alliancesRivals.value: Balances Russia, China and the West; a member of the CIS and the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation.

inventions.value: No major inventions are associated with the modern state.

scienceEducation.value: Universities in Tashkent and Samarkand, including the National University of Uzbekistan; literacy is high.

openness.value: Open to trade and foreign investment, with periods of restriction.

communicationTransport.value: Afrosiyob high-speed trains link Tashkent, Samarkand and Bukhara; Tashkent has a metro.

religion.value: Sources differ on the Muslim share: 94.28% (infobox, 2025), 96% (text), 96.7% (Pew projection) and 88% (CIA, 2004). The Hanafi school is not covered in the part read.

languageWriting.value: Uzbek is the official language, switched to Latin script in the 1990s; Russian is widely used.

artsArchitecture.value: Silk Road monuments such as the Registan in Samarkand and Khiva’s walled town, plus suzani embroidery and ikat silk.

socialStructure.value: Uzbek majority; Tajik and Russian minorities.

sharedIdentity.value: Uzbek identity built on Timur and Silk Road heritage, promoted by the state after 1991.

dailyLife.value: Family life in mahalla neighbourhoods; plov rice dish, round non bread and green tea.

ideasReligions.value: Revival of Sufi heritage such as the Naqshbandi order and its shrine near Bukhara, alongside a secular state.

colonisation.value: Part of the Russian Empire from the 1800s and the Soviet Union from the 1920s until 1991.

riseSignals.value: Declared independence from the Soviet Union on 31 August 1991.

peakPeriod.value: Too recent to judge; reforms since 2016 opened up the economy.

declineSignals.value: None that define the country as a whole.

outcome.value: Declared independence on 31 August 1991 after the failed Moscow coup; the infobox gives 1 September 1991.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
